events.title: R1/XCON: expert systems go commercial
events.summary: McDermott describes R1, a rule-based program built with Digital Equipment Corporation to configure VAX computer orders: turning a customer's order into a complete, valid set of components and how they fit together. The paper presents expert knowledge as something that can be captured in a large set of if-then rules, and treats R1's use in daily business at DEC as proof that this works in practice.
events.sourceNote: "R1 - A Rule-Based Configurer of Computer Systems"

events.title: Backpropagation popularized
events.summary: The paper shows that a multi-layer neural network can learn useful internal representations by propagating output errors backward through its layers and adjusting weights by gradient descent. Its historical importance is less the invention of the method than its framing: hidden units could discover features on their own, answering the objection that neural networks could not learn anything a single-layer perceptron could not.
events.sourceNote: "Learning representations by back-propagating errors"

events.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
events.summary: The builders' own account describes Deep Blue as a massively parallel search system: a general-purpose IBM supercomputer combined with hundreds of custom chess chips, able to evaluate hundreds of millions of positions per second. The paper presents its win as the result of specialized hardware, search, and a hand-tuned evaluation function, not as a machine that "thinks" about chess the way people do.
events.sourceNote: "Deep Blue"

events.title: Stochastic Parrots
events.summary: The paper argues that the NLP field's post-2018 turn toward ever-larger language models should not be narrated simply as technical progress. Larger models improve benchmark performance, but they also create environmental costs, access barriers, documentation debt, bias amplification, misleading claims about understanding, and downstream social harms.
events.sourceNote: "On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots - Can Language Models Be Too Big"

events.title: InstructGPT and RLHF
events.summary: This paper introduces InstructGPT: GPT-3 models fine-tuned to follow written instructions using supervised demonstrations and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The important historical move is that scale alone is explicitly separated from usefulness: the paper argues that next-token pretraining produces capability, but not necessarily instruction-following, truthfulness, harmlessness, or alignment with user intent.
events.sourceNote: "Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback"

events.title: ChatGPT launch
events.summary: OpenAI's launch post presents ChatGPT as a dialogue-oriented sibling of InstructGPT, trained through reinforcement learning from human feedback and released as a research preview. The post's historical importance is that it frames ChatGPT not as a sudden invention, but as an incremental product of GPT-3.5, InstructGPT, supervised dialogue data, reward modeling, PPO, user feedback, and iterative deployment.
events.sourceNote: OpenAI (2022) - Introducing ChatGPT

events.title: LLaMA released
events.summary: The article argues that Meta's LLaMA changed the large language model landscape by making a powerful foundation model available for research use in multiple sizes, including smaller models that required less computing infrastructure to study, retrain, and fine-tune. Its central historical problem is access: by early 2023, large language models had become technically important but institutionally concentrated because only a small number of organizations could afford to train and operate them. Meta presents LLaMA as a way to widen research participation while still managing risk through controlled, noncommercial access.
events.sourceNote: Introducing LLaMA - A foundational 65-billion-parameter large language model

events.title: LLaMA weights leak
events.summary: James Vincent argues that the leak of Meta’s LLaMA model marked a significant moment in the struggle over who should control access to powerful AI systems. The article explains a shift from large language models as guarded corporate or research assets toward models that could circulate through informal online networks, independent researchers, and open-source communities. What mattered was not simply that LLaMA was technically capable, but that its leakage exposed unresolved questions about AI safety, openness, institutional trust, and the political economy of access to expensive computational systems.
events.sourceNote: Meta’s powerful AI language model has leaked online — what happens now?

events.title: Google 'No Moat' memo
events.summary: The article republishes and contextualizes a leaked internal Google document arguing that the decisive shift in large language models in early 2023 was not simply OpenAI versus Google, but the rapid rise of open-source and semi-open AI development. The leaked author claims that cheaper fine-tuning methods, smaller models, quantization, leaked model weights, and distributed experimentation had undermined the assumption that frontier AI advantage depended mainly on enormous proprietary models and corporate secrecy. Historically, the article tries to explain why the center of AI innovation appeared to move, at least temporarily, from large firms with massive compute budgets toward a broader ecosystem of researchers, hobbyists, universities, startups, and open-source communities.
events.sourceNote: Google We Have No Moat And Neither Does OpenAI

events.title: Zuckerberg's open-source AI case
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg argues that advanced AI should develop through open-source ecosystems rather than closed proprietary platforms. The article frames Meta's Llama 3.1 release as an inflection point: open models, he claims, are becoming competitive with closed frontier systems while offering developers more control, lower costs, better customization, and less dependence on dominant vendors. Historically, the article tries to explain a platform transition: AI is becoming a foundational computing layer, and Zuckerberg argues that its dominant infrastructure should resemble Linux and other open-source systems rather than closed Unix-like or Apple-style ecosystems.
events.sourceNote: "Open Source AI is the Path Forward"

events.title: Kimi K3 released as open weights
events.summary: Cris Tolomia's article argues that Moonshot AI's release of Kimi K3 as a freely downloadable open-weight model marks a significant shift in the competitive organization of frontier AI. The central change is not only technical scale, though the model is described as unusually large, but a change in access: developers can download, adapt, self-host, and deploy the model outside the closed platforms of major U.S. firms. The article frames this as a business and geopolitical development, showing how openness can function as a market strategy, a challenge to proprietary AI systems, and a pressure point in U.S.-China technology rivalry.
events.sourceNote: China's Moonshot AI is releasing its record-setting open-weight model for free download

events.title: Kimi K3 renews the open-weight shift
events.summary: The article argues that Moonshot AI's release of Kimi K3 marked another moment when Chinese AI firms appeared to narrow the performance gap with leading U.S. labs, especially through large open-weight models. Its historical significance lies less in any single benchmark result than in what it reveals about changing AI competition: model capability, cost, access, compute constraints, national rivalry, and developer adoption are becoming intertwined. The article frames Kimi K3 as evidence that AI progress is no longer only about proprietary frontier systems from U.S. companies, but also about open-weight ecosystems, cheaper inference, and the tools that let developers swap models into applications.
events.sourceNote: Chinese AI has leveled up, and brought renewed focus on the open weight model shift

events.title: Chinese labs undercut U.S. costs
events.summary: Gordon argues that Chinese AI firms such as Moonshot AI, Z.ai, DeepSeek, Meituan, Tencent, Xiaomi, Alibaba, and MiniMax have narrowed the perceived gap with leading U.S. AI labs by producing models that are competitive in capability and dramatically cheaper to use. The article explains this shift as the result of constraint-driven engineering, open-source distribution, lower energy and infrastructure costs, domestic chip adaptation, and aggressive market positioning. Historically, the article is trying to explain why U.S. export controls and compute advantage did not preserve a stable American lead in AI, and why global users began treating Chinese models as practical infrastructure rather than second-tier alternatives.
events.sourceNote: "China's Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek are challenging U.S. AI labs-and beating them on cost"
